This video's account of Herbert Marcuse is inaccurate. Marcuse believed that capitalism in the West had become so good at satisfying human needs for those who participated in it that people willingly embedded themselves deep in its structure. Unlike the brutal sweatshop dominated version of capitalism that Marx knew when he formulated his ideas, this new capitalism gave people backyard pools, HD TVs, iPhones, and an entertainment economy that allowed all to feel they had expressed themselves. However, he ultimately believed that despite capitalism's new less brutally cruel incarnation, it trivialized culture and withered away people's critical faculties. The reason Marcuse emphasized marginalized people is because he thought that, since they were rejected by the seductive economy providing so much material wealth , they were the only class of people capable of forming a revolutionary class and overthrowing the bourgeoisie. Marcuse believed in the same revolution Marx did: the overthrow of the bourgeoisie by the proletariat and the creation of a classless society. He was simply describing how that might now be achieved.

This is a very subjective view. Typically speaking, looking through history as some things become easier, others become harder. For instance today in the US we have massive amounts of food available, but at the same time the amount of learning required just to survive is exponentially higher than for previous generations. We don't have to worry about bandits on the road killing us, but at the same time there is always a threat of a possible nuclear attack. Saying things are "better" is a subjective view based on opinion. If you wanted to live a simple life, its much more difficult to do so in todays modernized world compared to even 100 years ago. Not to mention that in todays world the rapid expansion of science and technology makes it very easy for a persons skill set and knowledge to become obsolete within their life, especially compared to the last 10,000 years where a persons skill set and knowledge very rarely would become obsolete within their lifetime. For instance a computer programmer who isn't retrained regularly will find themselves obsolete very quickly where as an old time blacksmith would be valuable for the entirety of their life, and often their skills would be passed through multiple generations with little in the way of change.

Another thing to consider is the speed of travel. In old times, diseases were fairly localized and could be easily contained. Things like the bird flu that originated in Asia likely would have never made it to Europe or the Americas in previous generations, where as today it can easily spread before detection across continents.

Objectively speaking, things aren't really better or worse for any generation, just different. You're great grandfather could easily support a family with a highschool education where in today's world that is nearly impossible without advanced tradeskills added to it. On the flipside your great grandfather would never had access to nearly as much knowledge in his entire lifetime as you can gain in a few weeks or even days in todays world. Life always will be a struggle of some sort, that wont ever change, what changes is what the struggle is.
